title: Mountcastle's Hypothesis
intro: Vernon Mountcastle proposed that the neocortex is built from one basic circuit repeated across the whole sheet, and that visual, auditory, motor and language areas differ mainly in what they are connected to, not in how they compute. If that is right, one well-designed column model could in principle serve every modality. This idea is the founding assumption of HTM and the Thousand Brains theory, so it is worth knowing exactly what the evidence supports and where it runs out.

blocks.text: Think of a computer cluster built from thousands of identical processors. One processor ends up doing vision only because a camera is plugged into it; another does audio only because a microphone is plugged in. Mountcastle's hypothesis says the cortex is like that: the 'processor' (a column) runs a common algorithm, and its specialisation comes from its inputs, outputs and experience. Hawkins & Blakeslee (2004) and Hawkins (2021) made this the starting point of their search for a single cortical algorithm.

In 'An organizing principle for cerebral function: the unit module and the distributed system' (Mountcastle 1978) and later in 'The columnar organization of the neocortex' (Mountcastle 1997), he argued that the neocortex is constructed from vertically organised modules — minicolumns grouped into columns — whose internal structure is broadly similar everywhere, and that the functional differences between areas arise from their different extrinsic connections. Note that this is two claims: an anatomical one (the local circuit repeats) and a computational one (it therefore performs the same operation everywhere). The second does not automatically follow from the first; the same hardware can run different software depending on parameters and learning.

items: The same six-layer pattern, the same excitatory projection classes (IT, ET/PT, CT) and the same interneuron families (PV, SST, VIP) occur in every neocortical area studied (see "Cell Types" and "Cortical Layers L1–L6").
Rockel, Hiorns & Powell (1980) reported a nearly constant number of neurons (about 110) in a narrow strip through the depth of cortex across areas and species, primate V1 excepted.

Tasic et al. (2018) found that GABAergic interneuron types in mouse visual cortex (VISp) and anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM) are largely shared, while many glutamatergic types are area-specific — a partial confirmation, discussed below.

blocks.text: The most striking evidence comes from Mriganka Sur's laboratory. In newborn ferrets, retinal axons were induced to innervate the auditory thalamus (MGN) by removing its normal inputs, so that auditory cortex received visual input. Roe et al. (1990) showed that the rewired auditory cortex developed visual receptive fields. Sharma, Angelucci & Sur (2000) showed that it developed orientation-selective neurons organised into an orientation map with pinwheels, resembling V1, although the map was less orderly and its horizontal connections differed from normal V1. Von Melchner, Pallas & Sur (2000) showed that the animals used the rewired cortex to see: light presented to the rewired pathway was perceived as visual rather than auditory.

items: In people blind from early life, occipital (visual) cortex is activated during Braille reading (Sadato et al. 1996), and disrupting it with TMS impairs Braille reading (Cohen et al. 1997).
Sensory substitution devices — e.g. vision delivered through tactile stimulation (Bach-y-Rita et al. 1969) — can be learned and used, suggesting that cortex can interpret new input streams.

These results show remarkable flexibility, but they do not prove the algorithm is identical everywhere: the recruited areas are typically higher-level or multisensory, and performance is usually worse than with the native modality.

Quantitative non-uniformity: Herculano-Houzel et al. (2008) found that neuron numbers per unit of surface vary several-fold across primate cortical areas, challenging the strict uniformity reported by Rockel et al. (1980).

Laminar differences: agranular motor and frontal areas have a strongly reduced L4, primate V1 has an elaborated L4, and layer thicknesses change systematically along the hierarchy (Harris & Shepherd 2015).

Area-specific cell types: some neurons exist only in particular areas or are greatly enriched there (e.g. Betz cells in primary motor cortex, von Economo neurons in anterior cingulate and frontoinsular cortex). Tasic et al. (2018) found most glutamatergic transcriptomic types differed between VISp and ALM.

Gradients: gene expression, dendritic spine counts on pyramidal cells, receptor densities and intrinsic timescales vary smoothly across the cortical hierarchy (e.g. Burt et al. 2018). Same circuit with different parameters may be the better description than identical circuits.

Rewiring is partial: the rewired ferret auditory cortex built a V1-like map, but a less orderly one, and behavioural vision through it was limited. Plasticity shows the circuit can adapt to new input, not that it is fully interchangeable.
Functional columns differ by species and area (see "Minicolumns and Columns"), so 'the column' as a unit is not uniform either.

blocks.text: A fair summary of current opinion: there is a canonical cortical circuit, in the sense of a shared set of cell types and a shared laminar wiring pattern, and it is plastic enough to process unfamiliar inputs. But areas tune that circuit — densities, layer sizes, cell-type proportions, time constants, receptor mixes — in systematic ways. Whether this tuning is 'the same algorithm with different hyperparameters' or 'different algorithms on similar hardware' is unresolved, and the answer may depend on how abstractly you define 'algorithm'.

Why the hypothesis matters for modellers even if it is only approximately true: it lets you develop and test one column model on one modality (e.g. touch or vision), then reuse it elsewhere. HTM (section 4) and the Thousand Brains theory (section 5) are explicit bets on this; the canonical microcircuit of Douglas, Martin & Whitteridge (1989) and the Bastos et al. (2012) predictive-coding microcircuit are related bets (section 6).
What this means for your model

items: Design for reuse: write one column class with its layer populations and learning rules, and let all modality-specific structure live in the encoder (your 'thalamus') and in the connectivity between columns. If your column only works with one input format, you have not tested the hypothesis.

Parameterise rather than hard-code: expose layer sizes, E:I ratios, time constants and L4 strength as parameters. Biology suggests areas differ in exactly these, so a 'motor' variant (small L4, large L5) should be a configuration, not a rewrite.

Test across modalities early: train the same column on two different input streams (for example MNIST images versus encoded audio or a sensorimotor touch task) — a cheap version of the ferret rewiring experiment.

Rely on learning for specialisation: the rewiring results suggest that input statistics plus plasticity produce area-specific tuning. STDP and homeostasis (section 3) are your mechanisms for that; hard-wired feature detectors work against the hypothesis.

Be honest about the assumption: in papers and notes, state that a common algorithm is a working hypothesis. Results that depend on it — such as voting between identical columns — inherit its uncertainty.
